question: Thousands of managers were each rated by bosses, peers and subordinates. How much of the variation in scores came from the raters themselves?
answer: More than half. Steven Scullen, Michael Mount and Maynard Goff found each rater's own tendencies, general impression and leniency included, outweighed the managers' actual performance, which explained only about a fifth. Bosses, peers and subordinates each had their quirks. A rating is largely a portrait of the person holding the pen.
move: Before reading a score as a measure of someone, ask who wrote it.
trap: Assuming a rating mostly measures the person being rated.
source: Scullen et al., Journal of Applied Psychology, 2000
reference: Scullen, Mount & Goff, Understanding the latent structure of job performance ratings, Journal of Applied Psychology, 2000
